claims.text: Conventionally cast or rolled HEAs generally have a relatively homogeneous, coarse-grained microstructure.
Severe plastic deformation introduces a high density of dislocations into the HEA.
Severe plastic deformation refines the HEA grain structure.
A short anneal near but below full recrystallization after severe plastic deformation will produce a bimodal distribution of ultrafine and coarser recrystallized grains.
Ultrafine grains increase strength through Hall–Petch grain-boundary strengthening.
Coarser grains within the bimodal structure maintain ductility by accommodating plastic deformation.
Coarser grains improve fracture resistance by promoting crack blunting and deflection.
Limited grain-boundary precipitates may impede crack growth.
The controlled anneal relaxes some residual stresses generated during deformation.
The controlled anneal can form beneficial metastable precipitates.
Residual-stress relaxation and metastable precipitates can modestly enhance effective Young’s modulus and toughness.
The proposed processing route will increase yield strength by approximately 10–20% relative to conventional processing.
The proposed processing route will maintain or slightly improve uniform elongation relative to conventional processing.
The proposed processing route will produce a modestly increased or more reliable effective Young’s modulus.
The proposed processing route will noticeably improve fracture resistance relative to conventional processing.
Insufficient deformation will fail to generate the defect density and heterogeneity needed for the desired hierarchical microstructure.
Excessive annealing will cause full recrystallization and eliminate the desired hierarchical microstructure and associated benefits.
An anneal that is too short will produce insufficient microstructural evolution for the claimed benefits.
